title: Service Decomposition

sections.title: Which Boundary Are We Trying to Establish?
Could the Boundary Stay Inside One Application?
Replacing Table Access With a Service Contract
What Happens When Catalog Is Unavailable?
Conditional Updates in an Owned API
Extracting the Dependency One Caller at a Time
Finding the Consumers That Rarely Run
Authorization After a Request Has Ended

html:
You can give two engineering teams separate repositories, separate deployment pipelines, and separate on-call rotations, yet a database change from one team can still stop the other team’s application. Baodium learned this during a Catalog release that seemed routine. A merchandising engineer added a column to the product table and started filling it with values from existing records. The migration had passed in staging. In production, checkout requests began waiting, and customers could no longer place orders.

Baodium had started as one Rails application maintained by five engineers. Catalog, Inventory, and Checkout shared a process and a PostgreSQL database. That arrangement suited the early team. A developer working on checkout could read the product tables directly, and several related changes could commit in one local transaction. As the company grew to forty engineers, the teams separated their code and release pipelines. Catalog became a service with its own deployment, while Order Service handled checkout. One dependency survived the split: Order Service still queried Catalog’s products table to check whether items in a cart could be sold.

During the merchandising migration, the Catalog team added a nullable display_weight column and backfilled it in the same database transaction. The schema alteration acquired an exclusive table lock, which was retained until the transaction finished. The backfill took much longer than the alteration, and checkout’s product reads queued behind the lock. For about thirty minutes, affected customers could not complete purchases.

Two days later, Catalog proposed another product-table change. The Checkout team wanted to review future migrations before they ran. Catalog objected because its engineers were supposed to own the product domain. You can see why both teams were concerned. Checkout needed dependable product eligibility checks, and Catalog needed to change how it stored product information without negotiating every internal column. Their release processes were separate, but their database contract had never been defined.

This is a useful point to revisit a familiar architectural question. When does a system benefit from another service, and what must change for the separation to mean anything? We’ll follow Baodium’s response, beginning with the immediate PostgreSQL mistake and then examining which responsibilities belonged on each side of the boundary.

Investigating the Database Lock

The first priority was restoring checkout. Extracting another service would not have helped customers waiting behind the migration transaction, so the on-call engineer began by examining PostgreSQL sessions and their blockers.

The query identifies sessions waiting behind other PostgreSQL processes. It helped the engineer connect Order Service’s delayed reads to the migration transaction rather than treating the problem as a general increase in query execution time. The migration’s ALTER TABLE had acquired an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which conflicts with ordinary reads. Once the backfill ran in that same transaction, the lock continued protecting the schema change for the duration of the backfill.

There was a related problem even before a waiting alteration acquired its lock. If an ALTER TABLE waits behind a long-running transaction, subsequent reads can queue behind the pending exclusive-lock request. A metadata-only change that would execute in milliseconds can therefore cause an extended outage when its lock cannot be acquired promptly.

Canceling the migration statement with pg_cancel_backend does not necessarily free the table. Inside an explicitly opened transaction, a statement error can leave the transaction aborted until its client issues a rollback. The locks are released when that transaction ends. Terminating the session with pg_terminate_backend ends its transaction and releases the locks, while discarding its uncommitted changes. During the incident, the responder had to establish which session owned the lock and which recovery action would end the transaction safely.

The correction was straightforward. The column would be added in a short transaction with a small lock_timeout. That transaction would commit before the backfill began. The backfill would use limited batches while the application tolerated rows whose new value was still null. The team would also monitor CPU, WAL generation, replica lag, and row-lock waits because small batches can still overload a busy database when they run too aggressively.

Migration frameworks differ in how they group statements into transactions. Baodium added a review check for that behavior rather than assuming that separate statements meant separate commits. It also set limits on idle transactions, since a client that starts a transaction and never finishes can obstruct schema maintenance even when it is not actively running a query.

That resolved the immediate failure mechanism. It did not resolve the argument between the teams. A future Catalog migration could still change or remove a column that Order Service depended on without Catalog knowing about the dependency. The engineers needed to identify what each team had actually gained when the application was split, and what was still shared.

Which Boundary Are We Trying to Establish?

Engineers often say they want to split a service when they mean several different changes. One may want independent deployments. Another may need separate database capacity. A third may want only Catalog to decide which product records are valid. These concerns are related, but the deployment layout does not resolve all of them at once.

Figure Figure illustrates the dependencies inside the earlier application, and Figure Figure shows what changes when components run separately.

Baodium had achieved release and runtime separation. Catalog’s process could crash without directly terminating Order Service, and the teams could build new images on independent schedules. Both applications still used the same product tables and database resources. An expensive Catalog query could compete with checkout for connections and I/O, while a schema change could prevent Order Service from executing its SQL at all.

Separate database schemas and roles could enforce who was permitted to read or change each domain’s tables while the applications continued sharing one PostgreSQL server. That would reduce accidental schema dependencies, but the same database instance would still have common CPU, storage, and maintenance limits. Dedicated database instances could isolate more of those resources. They would also need independent backup, replication, restore, credential, and capacity procedures. The team wanted evidence that the added separation would justify those responsibilities.

Could the Boundary Stay Inside One Application?

A smaller company might solve the same ownership problem without operating another networked service. Catalog could be a module that owns product records and exposes a limited interface to Checkout. Automated checks could reject an import that reached directly into Catalog’s persistence code. The application would retain local calls and the option to use one database transaction where that genuinely helped.

This is a modular monolith. In a Rails application, a tool such as Shopify’s Packwerk can check package dependencies. Java teams may use ArchUnit, while Python teams can use import-linter. The choice of tool matters less than whether a violation fails the build before the dependency becomes widespread.

We can test a proposed responsibility boundary cheaply inside one codebase. If it proves awkward, moving a module interface is usually easier than moving a production API and its database. An independent service becomes more compelling when a team needs its own deployment cycle, resources, security restrictions, or operating owner.

Baodium already had an independently deployed Catalog Service. The immediate decision was how Order Service should obtain the product facts and eligibility decisions it needed without reading Catalog’s tables.

Defining Ownership From Business Decisions

The teams first made an inventory of the product data Checkout used. A single products table contained fields serving several purposes. Some described the current listing. Others influenced whether an item could be purchased. Checkout also stored details of what a customer had agreed to buy. Those facts changed at different times and had different owners.

Consider a customer who ordered a jacket last month. The merchant may now change the listing title or withdraw it from sale. That does not change the description, price, and terms the customer accepted when placing the order. Checkout therefore records the accepted order-line details in its own database. Historical orders can be displayed from that record even when Catalog is unavailable or the listing has been retired.

The same distinction appears in billing and travel. An invoice retains the amount agreed when it was issued, and an airline booking records the fare purchased even after the published fare changes. In each case, the current catalog of offers and the accepted transaction have different lifetimes.

Domain-driven design calls an area in which a term has an agreed meaning a bounded context. Catalog’s product is the listing currently offered for sale. Checkout’s order line is a record of an accepted purchase. Making those meanings explicit allowed the teams to decide which data Checkout could copy and which decisions it still needed Catalog to make.

Keeping Invariants With Their Owners

Inventory provides a useful example. When one unit is reserved, the system must create the reservation and reduce the available quantity under the same correctness rule. Inventory Service owns that operation and performs its guarded update in one local transaction. Checkout requests a reservation and records the result. It does not fetch a quantity and later ask another service to decrement it, leaving a race between the two calls.

Sale eligibility introduced a subtler decision. A Catalog response might say that a jacket was eligible at 14:00:00, while a merchant withdrew it a moment later. Order Service could receive the earlier approval and commit the order after the withdrawal. Moving the query into a Catalog API would leave that race intact.

The product owner had to decide when the eligibility decision became binding. Baodium could issue an assessment valid for a particular checkout operation and input version until an explicit expiry, accepting the possibility that a later withdrawal would not cancel that assessment. Alternatively, a rule requiring every withdrawal to prevent all later order acceptance would need stronger coordination, such as a reservation of sale eligibility or a single owner enforcing the decision at commit. The correct choice depended on the business promise.

This is why ownership begins with operations and their guarantees. A service boundary cannot turn two independently committed databases into one transaction, and a network response does not establish that the underlying state cannot change afterward.

Decision review

What should Baodium separate first?

Order Service reads Catalog’s products table directly. A Catalog migration has interrupted checkout once. Catalog already has a separate process and release pipeline, but the teams have limited time for an extraction.

Move Catalog to a dedicated database immediately and replace every consumer during the same release.

Correct the migration procedure, introduce a Catalog-owned assessment contract, and remove Checkout’s direct table permission before considering a separate database.

Keep the table access and require Checkout to approve every future Catalog migration.

The second approach addresses the immediate locking risk and makes the ownership boundary enforceable before the larger data migration. It still leaves shared database resource contention and a required business dependency, which need testing. A dedicated database may later provide useful isolation, but combining every consumer migration and data cutover in one release creates a larger recovery problem. Requiring approval from Checkout can prevent a particular bad migration while leaving the same hidden schema dependency in place.

Replacing Table Access With a Service Contract

Order Service used the product table to decide whether each cart item could be accepted for sale. The first proposed API returned the complete product record so Order Service could continue interpreting the same columns. That would have moved the database dependency onto HTTP without giving Catalog control over the meaning of eligibility.

The teams instead defined one assessment operation for the cart. It accepted a bounded list of product references and relevant checkout attributes, then returned a decision for each item. Unknown products, ineligible products, and assessments that could not be completed were distinct outcomes. A timeout could not be interpreted as proof that a product was unknown or unavailable for sale.

POST /internal/catalog/eligibility-assessments HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"checkout_id":"co-4471","input_version":8,
 "items":[{"product_id":"p-12","quantity":1},
          {"product_id":"p-47","quantity":2}]}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"results":[
  {"product_id":"p-12","outcome":"eligible","version":21},
  {"product_id":"p-47","outcome":"ineligible","version":9}
]}

The example describes the interface between two trusted services. In the full API, the contract also defines the assessment’s validity period, quantity limits, error categories, and behavior when the input version changes. A batch-size limit prevents one request from assessing an unbounded cart.

Batching mattered to performance. Replacing one database query with ten network calls for a ten-item cart would increase dependency demand and the number of places a timeout could occur. One assessment reduced that chattiness and let Catalog apply its policy consistently.

The service identity tells Catalog which application is making the call. It still needs a trustworthy basis for the merchant and customer context used by the assessment. A caller cannot grant itself access to another merchant’s products by changing an identifier in the request body. Chapter 4 examined authenticated service calls and delegated identity, while Chapter 3 established why an operation ID is not an authorization.

Catalog published the contract in an OpenAPI specification and tested it against the requests and responses Order Service required. When Catalog changed its internal schema, the contract tests checked that the public operation still behaved as agreed. The same approach can be expressed through Protocol Buffers or another interface definition where that better fits the service’s communication pattern.

What Happens When Catalog Is Unavailable?

The new API gave the teams a stable interface, but the business still required an eligibility decision before accepting the order. A Catalog outage could therefore prevent new checkouts. The difference was that Order Service could now bound the call and return the agreed unavailable or pending outcome without occupying a database connection for an indefinite period.

Historical order pages used Checkout’s accepted order details and did not need that synchronous call. Browsing pages could use a local projection under a documented freshness policy. For a new purchase, the team did not silently substitute an old projected eligibility decision when the current policy required Catalog’s approval.

The team tested the failure contract while Catalog was unavailable. If an assessment could not be completed, Order Service refused or deferred order acceptance under the checkout API. It did not report a completed purchase merely because it had returned a fast HTTP response.

Conditional Updates in an Owned API

The contract also needed to support merchants editing configuration. Suppose two employees read shipping policy revision 7. One changes the permitted destinations, and the other changes the delivery cutoff. If both submit full replacements without a version check, the second update can silently erase the first.

HTTP provides a mechanism for this through an entity tag, or ETag, and the If-Match header.

GET /v1/merchants/42/shipping-policy HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "rev-7"

{"destinations":["US","CA"],"cutoff_hour":15}

PUT /v1/merchants/42/shipping-policy HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "rev-7"
Content-Type: application/json

{"destinations":["US","CA"],"cutoff_hour":16}

The server compares the supplied revision with its authoritative record inside the transaction that applies the update. If another employee has already committed revision 8, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed, and the client retrieves the new representation before resolving the conflict.1

This is optimistic concurrency control. It protects the meaning of one resource version. The idempotency key from Chapter 3 serves another purpose, allowing the application to recognize a repeated request for the same intended operation. A client may need both controls, particularly when it retries a conditional update after losing the response.

Extracting the Dependency One Caller at a Time

The teams agreed to remove Order Service’s direct product-table access before moving Catalog’s data. Figure Figure shows the main stages of that extraction.

The approach is often called the strangler pattern: new behavior replaces an older path incrementally while the surrounding system continues operating. For the eligibility query, Baodium divided the work into nine changes with explicit evidence before each promotion.

  1. Introduce a local adapter. Put Order Service’s product SQL behind CatalogClient. Verify that no direct product query remains elsewhere in Order Service.

  2. Define the operations. Replace per-item reads with the batch assessment while it is still a local call.

  3. Publish contract tests. Specify item outcomes, authorization, input limits, and unavailable behavior.

  4. Expose the remote endpoint. Catalog implements the assessment from its own process, initially using the same database.

  5. Compare both paths. The adapter evaluates the local and remote read-only implementations, returns the local result, and records mismatches under a bounded shadow-traffic budget.

  6. Move callers progressively. Route 1, then 10, then 100 percent of assessments to Catalog, watching correctness and checkout outcomes.

  7. Revoke direct permission. Remove Order Service’s access to the product tables and verify the denial in staging and production.

  8. Transfer data authority. Move Catalog’s authoritative records after the consumers and writers have been inventoried.

  9. Retire the compatibility path. Delete the local SQL implementation and temporary shadow comparison code.

The team ran the shadow comparison for seven days, including the weekly price import. Mismatches occurred in fewer than one per 100,000 assessments, and each was investigated. A low aggregate mismatch rate alone would not have been sufficient if the mismatches affected sale eligibility for a particular merchant or product category. The team checked those cases before moving customer traffic.

The shadow call also consumed resources, so it used a separate bounded allocation and never authorized a real order. Only the selected primary path provided the response used for checkout. The approach was appropriate for a read-only assessment, while shadowing a state-changing payment or reservation would require suppressing its effects.

Verifying the Permission Boundary

The seventh step was the point where the old dependency became unenforceable through normal application credentials. Catalog and Order Service already used distinct database roles, so the database could deny Order Service access to Catalog-owned tables.

The expected result is false. The engineer also checked the other affected tables and operations. A role can inherit access from another role or receive a grant through PUBLIC, so the team verified effective privileges rather than assuming one REVOKE statement had closed every path.

Permission removal was rehearsed first in staging. In production, the team watched for unexpected permission errors from applications and jobs. A failure in an overlooked reporting script would expose a dependency that the inventory had missed. The previous grant script was retained for a controlled reversal while the shared database was still authoritative.

Finding the Consumers That Rarely Run

Source search was useful for finding direct SQL, but it missed some administrative tools and scheduled tasks. Baodium examined database roles, query activity, imports, reporting jobs, foreign keys, and recovery scripts. Each dependency received an owner, a replacement, and evidence that the old access could be retired.

Consumer: Order Service
Existing access: SELECT products
Purpose: sale eligibility during order acceptance
Replacement: Catalog batch assessment
Unavailable outcome: defer or refuse acceptance
Owner: Checkout team
Retirement evidence: direct table access denied

With separate database roles, query statistics could help identify which application was reading a table. The pg_stat_statements extension records statements by database user, although its statistics are aggregated and may be reset. One week of activity cannot establish that a monthly job has no dependency. The inventory therefore combined runtime evidence with deployment configuration and conversations with the responsible teams.

Until this work finished, new cross-domain table access was prohibited. Otherwise, the teams could remove one hidden dependency while another application introduced a new one.

Transferring Catalog’s Data Authority

Order Service now used Catalog’s API. Catalog still stored its records in the shared PostgreSQL database. To isolate Catalog’s maintenance and resource demand, the team planned to move the authoritative product records to a separate database.

There would be a period when both databases contained copies of those records. The migration needed a single answer to a simple question: which database may accept a new product update right now? Chapter 7 established the same rule when Baodium moved one merchant between shards. Here the transfer involved an entire domain and its dependent records.

Copying the Existing Records

The team used PostgreSQL logical replication. A publication exposed the selected source tables, and a subscription copied their existing rows and then applied subsequent changes in commit order for the subscribed data. PostgreSQL coordinates the initial table synchronization with the change stream so writes committed during the copy are not simply omitted.2

A generic snapshot copied independently of change capture would not have that guarantee. A write committed after the snapshot but before the capture process began could disappear from the destination. The team therefore used the replication mechanism’s coordinated initialization rather than treating a bulk data export and a later stream as unrelated steps.

Logical replication also has limits. The destination needs a compatible table schema, indexes, constraints, and permissions provisioned separately. Sequence state is not advanced automatically by ordinary logical replication of table changes, so the team verified and advanced sequences before the new database began generating identifiers. Updates and deletes need an appropriate replica identity, and replication errors must be resolved before cutover.

The engineers compared records by primary key ranges and checked business relationships, including tenant ownership and product eligibility. Simple row counts would miss a case where one row was missing and another had been duplicated. Verification also needed a consistent source position, since comparing a current primary with a subscriber still catching up could report differences that were only replication delay.

Monitoring the Replication Slot

Logical replication depends on a replication slot at the publisher. The slot can cause WAL to be retained until the subscriber has advanced far enough. If the destination stops applying changes, retained WAL can grow on the source and eventually threaten its storage capacity.

Baodium monitored the slot’s retained WAL, subscriber errors, and apply progress. PostgreSQL’s max_slot_wal_keep_size can limit WAL retention at checkpoints, but reaching that limit can invalidate a lagging slot and force a recovery or resynchronization procedure. The team specified when it would pause or abandon the migration before the source ran out of space. A copy process intended to reduce coupling should not be allowed to take down the shared production database.

Until the transfer, source writes continued through the approved Catalog path. The destination served validation and migration operations, with no independent application writers. That prevented two competing histories from developing during the copy.

Moving Write Authority

For the final cutover, Baodium chose a short pause in product edits. Merchants could tolerate that interruption, and it gave the engineers a clear point after which no new source change should appear.

  1. Stop admitting new product writes through Catalog and every identified legacy writer.

  2. Finish or abort active source transactions, then fence old sessions and privileges so writes cannot restart.

  3. Record the final source change position after the writers are fenced.

  4. Apply all changes through that position to the destination, then verify records, constraints, and required relationships.

  5. Enable destination writes and change the Catalog connection configuration under the approved release procedure.

  6. Verify that every tested legacy write path is refused and that new writes reach only the destination.

Stopping new requests at the gateway was insufficient if an existing connection could still execute a transaction. Fencing covered pooled sessions, batch jobs, privileged tools, and any alternate writer. A credential change alone would not necessarily terminate an already connected session, which is why the team verified the old database’s actual write behavior before enabling the destination.

The recovery plan depended on the point of failure. Before destination writes began, the team could abandon the migration and return to the original source after verifying that it was still authoritative. Once the destination committed new product changes, the old database was an outdated copy. Reversing the connection string would lose those changes unless the team first performed a controlled transfer back. The test plan explicitly rehearsed interruptions before and after that authority change.

The original source copy was retained under restricted access for the verification period. Applications could not use it as a silent fallback. Reporting tools received approved exports or projections, while historical orders continued reading their accepted product details from Checkout.

Local Projections After Extraction

Once Catalog owned its writes, other services still needed product information for browsing and search. Requiring every consumer to call Catalog for every display field would increase synchronous dependencies, and many of those values did not need to be current to the millisecond.

The team published product changes through the transactional outbox from Chapter 3. Consumers maintained local projections: stored copies containing the fields and indexes suited to their own queries. Search could index product descriptions and categories. A browsing service could keep a small representation for product cards.

A projection needs a freshness contract. If a merchant updates a title, the browsing page may be permitted to show the earlier title briefly. A withdrawal that must immediately prevent checkout requires a different path. The projection’s existence does not change the authority of Catalog’s eligibility decision.

Each product change event carried a source version. The consumer applied an event only when its version was newer than the one already stored. That protected a product from an older event arriving after a newer one. The consumer also wrote its processing marker in the same local transaction as the projection update, so a crash could not record an event as processed while leaving the projection unchanged.

Version checks alone did not establish that every event had arrived. A consumer could be several versions behind and still process each event in order. The team monitored its progress through the source stream and used periodic reconciliation to detect missing records. A projection rebuild needed an initial snapshot aligned with its change stream, followed by catch-up and validation, just as the data migration had.

The application also defined a response when the projection exceeded its allowed freshness. Browsing could return a permitted unavailable or reduced result, while a required sale-eligibility decision continued through Catalog. Chapter 12 examines consumer ordering, replay, dead-letter handling, and recovery in greater depth.

Choosing the Next Service Boundary

After Catalog’s extraction, an architect proposed giving every major module its own service. The diagram looked tidy: pricing, promotions, notifications, search, and refunds each received a box. The senior engineers wanted to know what would improve for customers and teams before accepting the additional deployment and operating costs.

Every independently operated service needs credentials, capacity planning, telemetry, incident ownership, and a recovery procedure. Callers inherit network failure, timeout, and version-compatibility concerns. Data copied across boundaries needs a repair policy. Some separation is justified by scale or security, while other separation creates coordinated releases for code that previously changed together.

Baodium considered the next candidates against their operations. Inventory needed one owner for reservation and quantity updates, so that transaction boundary was preserved. Notifications could run after order acceptance and consume an outbox event, which made independent failure and retry behavior useful. A tightly interleaved pricing calculation could remain an internal module until it needed its own capacity or release cycle.

This evaluation applies outside commerce. Consider an internal platform that publishes deployment policies, evaluates changes, checks approvals, notifies Slack, and records an audit history. Five functions do not necessarily require five services.

A first implementation can place policy publication, evaluation, approval, and audit records in separate modules backed by one PostgreSQL database. The policy module owns immutable published revisions, while an outbox worker sends notifications. Jenkins calls the enforcement API when it attempts a deployment, and Slack displays the result. Neither Jenkins nor Slack becomes an independent authority for what policy is active.

If the integration workload later needs its own scaling or credential boundary, the team can extract the delivery worker. It may own connector attempts and status, while the policy owner continues controlling the revision contents and the authorization decision. The contract specifies which events and identities cross that boundary, without giving the integration service permission to rewrite policy history.

This is a more useful way to decide whether to extract another service. The team can identify the decision that requires independent ownership, the resource or release dependency it wants to remove, and the costs of operating the new boundary.

Authorization at Service Boundaries

Service decomposition also changes where permissions are enforced. Suppose a merchant employee requests a refund. Order Service knows the merchant associated with the order, while Payment Service owns refund operations. The gateway can authenticate the employee, but those facts do not, by themselves, authorize a refund.

Order Service can check whether the employee is permitted to view or act on the order. Payment Service still verifies the payment’s current state, merchant ownership, refund amount, and the permission required for that financial action before it records a refund operation.

An event called RefundRequested describes an instruction to consider. A later RefundCompleted event reports a result the owning service has committed. A consumer must not interpret either event as permission to perform another unrelated operation. The producer’s identity and the event schema establish provenance, while the receiving service’s policy determines which action is permitted.

Tenant-Scoped Reads

Consider an employee changing the order ID in a request from 4471 to 4472. If Order Service checks only that the employee has a merchant role, it could return a record belonging to another merchant. The resource relationship needs to be part of the authorization check.

After resolving merchant membership from trusted server-side data, the service can include that merchant in its database query.

The merchant ID is derived from the authenticated principal’s permitted scope rather than copied from an untrusted request field. That prevents an order ID by itself from selecting another merchant’s record. A successful read still does not grant refund permission, which requires its own action-specific checks.

PostgreSQL row-level security can add a database enforcement boundary. With pooled connections, tenant context must be assigned and reset safely, for example through transaction-local settings and tested role policies. A setting leaked from one request to another would turn a protection mechanism into a cross-tenant access risk.

Distinct workload identities and scoped database roles also prevent Order Service from changing Payment Service’s refund table directly. If two services share unrestricted credentials, the diagram may show an ownership boundary that the database cannot enforce.

Authorization After a Request Has Ended

A deferred refund may run after the employee’s browser session expires or their permission changes. The background worker authenticates as a service, while the original approval belongs to a particular employee, merchant, payment, amount, and operation identity. Chapter 4 established why the workflow needs a rule for approval expiry and revocation before dispatch.

If current permission evidence is required and its provider is unavailable, the worker retains the refund in a pending or review state. It cannot convert missing evidence into authorization. Likewise, an idempotency key ensures the request can be recognized during retries, while access to the underlying operation is still checked on every status or recovery request.

Verifying That Extraction Was Worthwhile

Baodium tested the new boundaries under the failures that had motivated the project. It ran a blocking Catalog migration in staging and verified that checkout used its bounded assessment call rather than issuing product SQL. When Catalog was unavailable, historical orders still displayed from Checkout’s records, and new orders requiring current eligibility received the documented incomplete outcome.

The team then checked database permissions using Order Service’s actual credentials. Direct product-table reads failed, including from older application images and scheduled jobs. The ownership-transfer rehearsal confirmed that every accepted source write reached the destination and that no tested interruption left both databases authorized to write the same product records.

Projection tests delayed events, delivered them out of order, and rebuilt records from a source snapshot. The receiving services had to avoid applying older versions and recognize when their copies no longer met the freshness requirement. Security tests used an employee from one merchant to request another merchant’s records and refunds, including through the new remote APIs and deferred workers.

The engineers also measured ordinary development. Could Catalog change an internal table without asking Order Service to deploy? Did a broken API response fail consumer contract tests? Could the two teams investigate a failed checkout using their own telemetry and shared operation identity, without unrestricted access to each other’s data?

Those were the outcomes the extraction had been intended to improve. Catalog now controlled its product schema and database, while Checkout relied on a documented decision contract and its own accepted-order records. New orders still depended on Catalog when a current eligibility decision was required. That dependency was an explicit business choice, with a measured failure response and an accountable owner.

Summary

The Catalog migration interrupted checkout because an exclusive table lock continued through a long backfill, and Order Service still queried Catalog’s product tables. The immediate correction was a safer migration. The architectural correction took longer: Catalog and Checkout agreed on who owned each decision, replaced direct SQL with a bounded contract, and verified that database permissions prevented the old access.

Moving Catalog’s records required another controlled change. The engineers copied the data, applied subsequent updates, fenced the source writers, and verified the destination before transferring authority. Other services could maintain local projections for permitted reads, while current sale eligibility continued to follow its business contract.

The same decisions apply when separating billing from subscriptions, booking from inventory, or policy enforcement from notification delivery. A useful service boundary establishes who may change a record, which operations callers may request, and what happens when the owner is unavailable. In Chapter 12, we’ll follow the events that cross those boundaries and examine what consumers must do when messages arrive late, are delivered twice, or require replay.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Catalog and Checkout can deploy independently once Checkout uses an owned eligibility contract and no longer accesses Catalog’s product tables.
Condition that tests it & A Catalog migration blocks product reads, a required assessment is unavailable, or a legacy consumer attempts direct table access.
Constraint or invariant & Catalog owns product writes and eligibility decisions. Checkout owns accepted order details. Inventory owns reservation transactions. At any point in a database transfer, exactly one source has write authority.
Evidence and uncertainty & Contract comparisons and permission tests verify the new boundary. Migration rehearsals check final change delivery and source fencing.

Still unknown: how often Catalog availability will interrupt new orders and which additional reads can safely use delayed projections.
Signal and evaluation window & During extraction and failure tests, measure contract mismatches, direct access failures, assessment latency, migration catch-up, and incorrect or stale projection results.
Control and decision & Correct blocking migrations before extraction. Remove direct permissions, transfer authority only after verification, and keep required purchase decisions under the owner’s contract.
Owner and review trigger & Catalog owns the schema, assessment API, and data transfer. Checkout owns caller behavior and accepted orders. Product and security owners approve eligibility and access rules. Review after coordinated-release incidents or before another domain extraction.
